extracted.intended_audience: physicians, AMA members, medical societies, policymakers, and legal advocates interested in Medicare rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes and advocates the position that the Department of Health and Human Services/CMS must follow the Medicare statute requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking, explaining why that process is necessary and giving examples where skipping it produced harms. Useful for readers evaluating procedural requirements for Medicare regulatory changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicare statute requires notice-and-comment rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief calls on the court to require that the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees CMS, follow the Medicare statute that requires notice-and-comment rulemaking even if it seems burdensome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even seemingly small or burdensome decisions that modify reimbursement determinations should go through the notice-and-comment process; procedural compliance is required by statute regardless of administrative convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment facilitates public input and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: “Notice-and-comment rulemaking facilitates public input into agency decision-making, as well as greater transparency and clarity on the part of the agency,” the brief states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process should be used to allow the public and stakeholders to see proposed rules, comment, and thereby increase clarity about agency intentions and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-comment serves as a check on administrative power
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief argues notice-and-comment provides an important check against unbridled administrative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should not bypass the process because doing so reduces external oversight and the accountability that public participation provides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulsome public input is essential given Medicare’s scope and stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Because the administration of Medicare implicates the health of millions of Americans, fulsome opportunities for public input are essential.” Medicare pays for 20 percent of health care in the U.S.; many physicians treat Medicare patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a program affects large populations and core health services, agencies should prioritize robust public engagement before implementing changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder expertise must inform rulemaking (agency education and responsiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment gives stakeholders a chance to voice opinions, let CMS have relevant facts, and let expert stakeholders offer alternative solutions. “This exchange of information enables the agency promulgating the rule to educate itself before establishing rules and procedures… It also increases the likelihood of administrative responsiveness to the needs and concerns of those affected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should solicit and meaningfully consider technical facts, operational experience, and alternative proposals from regulated parties to produce better-informed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant financial consequences demand procedural protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Even ‘seemingly minor’ modifications in reimbursement determinations give rise to extreme financial consequences for providers and patients; the contested payment-method change was estimated to affect $3–4 billion in Medicare payments over nine years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a regulatory change has large fiscal impacts, agencies should be required to follow formal rulemaking procedures (notice-and-comment) to surface and address financial and practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skipping notice-and-comment can create unclear, unfair, and inconsistent rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The brief cites real-world examples where HHS bypassed notice-and-comment, creating unclear rules that produced unfairness and inconsistency for physicians and beneficiaries (examples: the two-midnight rule and national versus local coverage determinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid issuing interpretive guidance or ad hoc changes without public process; such shortcuts can produce administrability problems and disparate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations subject to notice-and-comment are higher-quality and more administrable
rubrics_metrics.description: As a comparison, the brief notes that regulations that undergo notice-and-comment rulemaking are of higher quality and have improved administrability. Example: HHS publishes a Medicare fee schedule annually; the AMA analyzes and comments, and HHS considers and incorporates AMA’s comments when drafting the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the iterative back-and-forth of notice-and-comment to improve clarity, practical implementation, and effectiveness of final rules; centralized dialog with stakeholders can be accomplished within months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer more formal rulemaking for Medicare (not less)
rubrics_metrics.description: “More rather than less formal rulemaking for Medicare is warranted,” the brief concludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, agencies should opt for full notice-and-comment procedures for Medicare policies rather than relying on less formal approaches that limit public participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural compliance is distinct from substantive disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Litigation Center brief does not address how a hospital payment should be calculated; instead it focuses on the importance that HHS follow notice-and-comment statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal challenges about procedural compliance can and should be pursued separately from debates over the substantive merits of a policy; even disputed policy choices must be adopted through lawful procedures.
